## Overview

The western corn rootworm *Diabrotica virgifera virgifera* lays its eggs in
maize, and its larvae feed on the roots of the next year's maize. Rotating a
field to another crop starves them, so rotation is the main defence, and in
parts of Europe the law has required it. @Szalai2014 asked how much rotation a
region needs, and whether such laws help, with a lattice model of a whole
agricultural region:

- each cell is a field, on a torus of 100 × 100;
- each year a field is in another crop, first-year maize or continuous maize,
  and changes at random with probabilities chosen so that the shares of maize
  and of rotated maize stay as set;
- rootworms grow only in continuous maize, and their populations in a field
  rotated out of maize are lost;
- each year a share of the adults, rising with their density, leaves each
  continuous maize field for the maize fields within its dispersal range;
- a field counts as at risk when its density exceeds the economic threshold.

This implementation is a **reproduction** of the authors' R script, published
with the article; run side by side, the two agree in distribution.

```{julia}
#| output: false
ENV["GKSwstype"] = "100"
using EcologicalCellularAutomata
using CellularAutomataCore
using Plots
using Statistics
```

## The crops

The probabilities of staying in or turning to maize keep the shares fixed. A
field in another crop is sown with maize with probability `pE`, first-year
maize stays maize with `pF` and continuous maize with `pC`; the farmers'
decision factor `Q = pF / pC` says whether they prefer to rotate young or old
maize. Laws that end maize after three, four or five years change `pC`, which
the script finds as the root of a polynomial.

```{julia}
[(; policy, rotated,
  probabilities=round.(values(rootworm_probabilities(0.4, 1 - rotated, 1.0, policy)); digits=3))
 for policy in 0:3 for rotated in (0.4, 0.6)
 if rootworm_probabilities(0.4, 1 - rotated, 1.0, policy) !== nothing]
```

With 40% of the fields in maize and the other parameters at the most likely
values of the source's Table 1, a run shows the crops and the rootworms after
dispersal in the first and the tenth year:

```{julia}
sol = solve(problem(:rootworm_rotation; rotated=0.6, seed=1))
crops(u) = [c == 0 ? 0 : c == 1 ? 1 : 2 for c in u.crop]
plot(heatmap(crops(sol.u[end]); c=cgrad([:wheat, :lightgreen, :darkgreen], 3; categorical=true),
             title="crops, year 10", colorbar=false),
     heatmap(log10.(sol.u[1].pop .+ 0.01); clims=(-2, 2), title="log10 density, year 1"),
     heatmap(log10.(sol.u[end].pop .+ 0.01); clims=(-2, 2), title="log10 density, year 10");
     layout=(1, 3), size=(1000, 300), aspect_ratio=1, ticks=false, titlefontsize=9)
```

The output of a run is the share of maize fields above the threshold, averaged
over years 2 to 10.

## Rotation and the law

The source's Fig. 5 shows that output against the share of rotated maize,
with all other parameters at their most likely values, without legislation and
with rotation required after three, four or five years of maize. Ten runs at
each point:

```{julia}
rots = 0.3:0.05:0.8
labels = ["no legislation", "after 3 years", "after 4 years", "after 5 years"]
curves = Vector{Vector{Float64}}(undef, 4)
Threads.@threads for k in 1:4
    policy = (0, 1, 2, 3)[k]
    curves[k] = [rootworm_probabilities(0.4, 1 - r, 1.0, policy) === nothing ? NaN :
                 mean(rootworm_output(solve(problem(:rootworm_rotation; rotated=r, policy,
                                                    seed=s))) for s in 1:10)
                 for r in rots]
end
plot(100 .* rots, [100 .* c for c in curves]; label=permutedims(labels), lw=2, marker=:circle,
     ms=3, xlabel="rotated maize (%)", ylabel="maize fields above threshold (%)",
     legend=:bottomleft, size=(650, 400))
```

As in the source, nearly every maize field is above the threshold when less
than about 40% of the maize is rotated, and few are above it when more than
about 75% is. A law ending maize after three years needs the least rotation;
after four years, a little less than none; after five years, about the same as
none. The curves sit a few points of rotation to the right of the source's
Fig. 5 (about 44% of fields above the threshold at 65% rotated without
legislation,
against about 35% read from the figure). The authors' own script, run with the
same parameters, does the same, so the figure presumably used other values.

## The script and this model

Run 100 times each at 13 points of these curves, the script and this model
give the same distributions of the output, and of its shares in first-year and
continuous maize: the correlations of their empirical distribution functions
are 0.97–1.00, 38 of the 39 Kolmogorov–Smirnov distances lie below the 5%
critical value, and the means differ by at most 0.05 (0.652 in both at 60%
rotated without legislation).

## Field size and dispersal range

Dispersal reaches the fields within the range divided by the side of a field.
The source's Fig. 6 compares fields of 2 and 100 ha, and ranges of 1 and 3 km:

```{julia}
rots6 = 0.5:0.05:0.75
variant(; kw...) = [mean(rootworm_output(solve(problem(:rootworm_rotation; rotated=r, seed=s,
                                                        pmap=(; kw...)))) for s in 1:10)
                    for r in rots6]
fig6 = [variant(; fieldsize=2.0), variant(; fieldsize=100.0), variant(; range=1000.0),
        variant(; range=3000.0)]
plot(plot(100 .* rots6, [100 .* fig6[1] 100 .* fig6[2]]; label=["2 ha" "100 ha"],
          title="field size"),
     plot(100 .* rots6, [100 .* fig6[3] 100 .* fig6[4]]; label=["1 km" "3 km"],
          title="dispersal range");
     xlabel="rotated maize (%)", ylabel="maize fields above threshold (%)", lw=2, marker=:circle,
     ms=3, layout=(1, 2), size=(850, 350), titlefontsize=10, left_margin=4Plots.mm,
     bottom_margin=4Plots.mm)
```

Larger fields and shorter ranges leave some maize fields out of the reach of
others, and so slightly fewer above the threshold, as the source found.
